chapter: 18 Best practices for the real world

questions.question: What two limitations of the book's models so far does the chapter introduction point out?
questions.answer: They were trained at small scale (small datasets, a single GPU), and they generally did not reach the best achievable performance on their datasets.
questions.explanation: Both are stated in the second paragraph.

questions.question: Sort the five topics into 'better model quality' and 'faster/bigger compute'.
questions.answer: Quality: hyperparameter tuning, model ensembling. Compute: multi-GPU/TPU training, mixed-precision training, quantization.
questions.explanation: This matches the chapter outline: 18.1 vs 18.2-18.3.

questions.question: Which of the following is a parameter rather than a hyperparameter, in the book's terms?
options: The number of units in a Dense layer
The dropout rate
A weight in a Dense layer's kernel
Whether to use BatchNormalization after a layer
questions.answer: A weight in a Dense layer's kernel
questions.explanation: Parameters are trained via backpropagation; kernel weights are learned. Units, dropout rate and the BatchNormalization decision are architecture-level choices the page lists as hyperparameters.

questions.question: List the six steps of the typical hyperparameter optimization process.
questions.answer: 1) Choose hyperparameters automatically; 2) build the model; 3) fit on training data and measure on validation data; 4) choose the next hyperparameters automatically; 5) repeat; 6) eventually measure performance on test data.
questions.explanation: Reproduced from the numbered list on the page.

questions.question: Why does step 3 use validation data while test data is reserved for step 6?
questions.answer: The search picks configurations based on the feedback signal, so whatever data provides it gets indirectly fit. Using validation data for selection and touching the test set only at the end keeps an unbiased estimate of generalization.
questions.explanation: This is the information-leak argument from chapter 5 (p.173) and the summary's warning about validation-set overfitting (p.587).

questions.question: The authors say tuning 'is better left to a machine'. What two arguments on the page support automating it?
questions.answer: There are no formal rules and even good intuition yields suboptimal initial choices; and hand-tweaking and retraining consumes most of engineers' time, so a systematic, principled automated search is both better and less wasteful.
questions.explanation: Both points appear in the 'In practice...' paragraph.

questions.question: What does section 18.1 aim for, in the authors' words?
options: Something that works okay
Works great and wins machine learning competitions
The smallest possible model
Training on a single GPU
questions.answer: Works great and wins machine learning competitions
questions.explanation: The section intro contrasts 'works okay' (blind trial and error) with 'works great and wins machine learning competitions'. The other options are not its goal.

questions.question: Think of a model you trained earlier in the book. Which of its settings were hyperparameters, and which would you put in a search space first?
questions.answer: Open-ended, e.g. number of Dense units, number of layers, dropout rate, learning rate.
questions.explanation: Being able to name hyperparameters in your own models is the first step toward defining a search space (p.564).

questions.question: Why can't you usually use gradient descent to optimize hyperparameters?
options: Hyperparameters have too many dimensions
The hyperparameter space is typically made of discrete decisions and isn't continuous or differentiable
Gradient descent only works on the test set
KerasTuner does not support gradients
questions.answer: The hyperparameter space is typically made of discrete decisions and isn't continuous or differentiable
questions.explanation: This is the first bullet. Dimensionality is not the issue (weights have far more dimensions); the test set is irrelevant; the limitation is mathematical, not a library restriction.

questions.question: Which values can hp.Int(name="units", min_value=16, max_value=64, step=16) return, and how many configurations does the full search space have once the optimizer Choice of p.565 is added?
questions.answer: 16, 32, 48, 64; with optimizer ∈ {rmsprop, adam}, 4 × 2 = 8 configurations.
questions.explanation: The range includes max_value with step 16. The optimizer Choice has two values (p.565).

questions.question: Explain the 'noisy feedback' challenge and one way to mitigate it.
questions.answer: Training is stochastic, so a small difference such as 0.2% may come from lucky initialization rather than a better configuration. Mitigate by training each configuration several times and averaging (KerasTuner's executions_per_trial).
questions.explanation: The page raises the problem; p.566 introduces executions_per_trial to reduce metric variance.

questions.question: What must a KerasTuner model-building function return?
options: An uncompiled model
A compiled Keras model
A dictionary of hyperparameters
The validation accuracy
questions.answer: A compiled Keras model
questions.explanation: The page says it 'returns a compiled Keras model'. The tuner, not the function, trains and measures accuracy; hyperparameters come from hp.

questions.question: Name three techniques the page lists for choosing the next set of hyperparameters.
questions.answer: Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, simple random search.
questions.explanation: Listed in the first paragraph.

questions.question: Why is computing the feedback signal for hyperparameter optimization so expensive compared with computing a gradient for weight training?
questions.answer: Each evaluation requires creating and training a new model from scratch on the dataset, while a gradient step needs only the loss on one mini-batch and a backward pass.
questions.explanation: Contrast between paragraph 2 and bullet 2.

questions.question: Take a model you wrote earlier and rewrite one hardcoded value as an hp.Int or hp.Choice call. What range would you choose and why?
questions.answer: Open-ended; e.g. units=hp.Int('units', 32, 256, step=32), around the value that worked previously.
questions.explanation: Practicing the hardcoded-to-range conversion is the key idea of KerasTuner.

questions.question: Which hyperparameter types does the Listing 18.1 callout say are available in KerasTuner?
options: Int, Float, Boolean, Choice
Int, String, List, Dict
Discrete, Continuous, Random
Units, Optimizer, Loss
questions.answer: Int, Float, Boolean, Choice
questions.explanation: The callout lists exactly these four. The other options are invented categories or specific settings, not KerasTuner types.

questions.question: What is the only functional difference between SimpleMLP.build and build_model?
questions.answer: The output layer uses self.num_classes (set in the constructor) instead of the hardcoded 10.
questions.explanation: The callout says build is identical to build_model; num_classes is the configurable constant.

questions.question: Why is num_classes passed to the constructor rather than sampled from hp?
questions.answer: It is a property of the task, not a design choice to optimize. Constructor arguments configure model constants, while hp is reserved for values the tuner should search.
questions.explanation: The callout: the object-oriented approach lets you configure model constants as constructor arguments instead of hardcoding them.

questions.question: Describe the three things a tuner does on each iteration of its loop.
questions.answer: Pick a set of hyperparameter values; call the model-building function with them to create a model; train the model and record its metrics.
questions.explanation: These are the three bullets at the bottom of the page.

questions.question: Why does Listing 18.1 use loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy"?
options: The labels are integer class indices and the output is a 10-way softmax
The labels are one-hot vectors
It is a binary classification problem
It makes training faster than any other loss
questions.answer: The labels are integer class indices and the output is a 10-way softmax
questions.explanation: Sparse categorical crossentropy expects integer labels with a softmax over classes. One-hot labels would use categorical_crossentropy; binary problems use binary_crossentropy; speed is not the reason.

questions.question: Assuming 784 input features, how many trainable parameters does the model have when units = 32?
questions.explanation: Dense parameters = inputs × units + units (biases), for each layer. (The 784-feature input is an assumption for MNIST; the listing has no explicit Input.)

questions.question: Could you convert your own model-building function into a HyperModel subclass, moving at least one constant into the constructor?
questions.answer: Open-ended.
questions.explanation: Doing this exercise checks that you understand the split between fixed constants and tunable hyperparameters.

questions.question: What distinguishes BayesianOptimization from RandomSearch in KerasTuner, according to the page?
options: It trains each model with Bayesian neural networks
It predicts which new hyperparameter values are likely to perform best given previous outcomes
It uses gradient descent on the hyperparameters
It trains many models briefly and keeps only the best ones
questions.answer: It predicts which new hyperparameter values are likely to perform best given previous outcomes
questions.explanation: The book describes BayesianOptimization as making smart predictions from the outcomes of previous choices. It does not change the models themselves (option 1). Hyperparameter spaces are not differentiable, so gradient descent is not used (option 3, p.564). Option 4 describes Hyperband.

questions.question: With max_trials=20 and executions_per_trial=2, what is the maximum number of model training runs the search performs, and why does executions_per_trial exist?
questions.answer: Up to 40 runs (20 × 2). Repeated executions are averaged to reduce the variance of the metric.
questions.explanation: Each trial trains the same configuration executions_per_trial times from scratch, and the tuner averages the results, as the callout explains.

questions.question: Why does the callout insist on using a validation metric such as val_accuracy as the objective?
questions.answer: The search should find configurations that generalize. Training metrics reward capacity and memorization, so a tuner optimizing them would pick overfitting models.
questions.explanation: The callout says: 'Always specify validation metrics since the goal of the search process is to find models that generalize!' This links back to the train/validation/test discussion on p.173.

questions.question: In the search_space_summary() output, what does 'Default search space size: 2' refer to?
options: The number of trials already run
The number of hyperparameters defined (units and optimizer)
The number of possible model configurations
The number of executions per trial
questions.answer: The number of hyperparameters defined (units and optimizer)
questions.explanation: Two hyperparameters are listed below the header. The number of configurations is the product of their possible values, much more than 2. Trials and executions are unrelated to this summary.

questions.question: When should you set overwrite=False on the tuner?
questions.answer: When you want to resume a previously started search (for example after a crash) with the same model-building function, reusing the logs in the directory.
questions.explanation: The callout says to set overwrite to True if the model-building function changed (start fresh) and to False to resume. p.567 repeats this for crashed searches.

questions.question: Why can KerasTuner infer the direction for 'val_accuracy' but not for a custom metric?
questions.answer: It knows the semantics of built-in metric names (accuracy up, loss down). An arbitrary custom metric could be either 'higher is better' or 'lower is better', so you must declare it with kt.Objective.
questions.explanation: This is the content of the 'Objective maximization and minimization' sidebar; the explicit form appears on p.567.

questions.question: Compare the units range printed by search_space_summary() with the one in listing 18.1. Do they agree? What would you expect to see if you ran the book's code?
questions.answer: They disagree: the summary shows 128-1024 step 128, the listing defines 16-64 step 16. Running the book's code would print min_value 16, max_value 64, step 16.
questions.explanation: The summary is a direct readout of the hp.Int call. The difference suggests the printed output came from a different version of the code.

questions.question: What does the name argument of kt.Objective refer to?
options: The Python variable holding the metric object
The metric's name as found in the epoch logs
The name of the tuner's log directory
The name of the hyperparameter being optimized
questions.answer: The metric's name as found in the epoch logs
questions.explanation: The callout says the name is the metric's name 'as found in epoch logs', e.g. 'val_accuracy'. It is not a Python object, a directory or a hyperparameter.

questions.question: How many samples are used for training, validation and testing during the search, and which array is reserved for later?
questions.answer: 50,000 train, 10,000 validation (the last 10,000 of the original training set), 10,000 test. x_train_full / y_train_full (all 60,000) are reserved for the final retraining.
questions.explanation: num_val_samples = 10000 is sliced off the end of the 60,000-sample training set; the test set is MNIST's official 10,000 samples.

questions.question: Why would using the test set as validation data during the search make the test metrics untrustworthy?
questions.answer: The tuner picks configurations that score best on the validation data. If that is the test set, the chosen model is selected to fit the test set, so its test score overestimates performance on truly new data.
questions.explanation: Selection is a form of training at the hyperparameter level. This is the information-leak argument of p.173 and the validation-overfitting note on p.569.

questions.question: Why does the search use epochs=100 together with an EarlyStopping callback?
options: Because MNIST always needs exactly 100 epochs
Because you don't know in advance how many epochs each model will need, so training stops when it starts overfitting
Because KerasTuner requires at least 100 epochs
To make each trial take the same amount of time
questions.answer: Because you don't know in advance how many epochs each model will need, so training stops when it starts overfitting
questions.explanation: This is the callout's explanation. MNIST has no fixed epoch requirement, KerasTuner has no minimum, and early stopping makes trial durations vary.

questions.question: Your 3-day search crashes after 30 hours. What do you change to continue it?
questions.answer: Recreate the tuner with the same directory and model-building function but overwrite=False, then call tuner.search() again; it resumes from the trial logs on disk.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph after the code and in the overwrite callout on p.566.

questions.question: The early-stopping callback monitors val_loss while the tuner's objective is val_accuracy. Is that a problem?
questions.answer: Not usually. Both measure validation performance and tend to improve together, but they can diverge (a model can become overconfident, so val_loss rises while val_accuracy stays flat). In that case a run may stop slightly before its best val_accuracy.
questions.explanation: Beyond the book: loss is a smoother signal and is the conventional choice for early stopping, while accuracy is the metric the tuner ranks on.

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, what each of the four arrays x_train, x_val, x_test, x_train_full is used for in the full tuning workflow?
questions.answer: x_train: fit each trial; x_val: objective and early stopping; x_test: final evaluation only; x_train_full: retrain the selected configurations.
questions.explanation: See the breakdown table in the deeper section and p.569 for the retraining.

questions.question: What does tuner.get_best_hyperparameters(top_n) return?
options: The top_n trained Keras models
A list of HyperParameters objects that can be passed to the model-building function
The validation accuracies of the top_n trials
A new tuner restricted to the top_n configurations
questions.answer: A list of HyperParameters objects that can be passed to the model-building function
questions.explanation: The listing's callout says exactly this. Trained models come from get_best_models (p.569); scores and a new tuner are not what this method returns.

questions.question: Why is it acceptable to train the final models on the validation data?
questions.answer: No further hyperparameter decisions will be made, so validation data is no longer needed for evaluation. It becomes extra training data, while the separate test set still gives an unbiased final estimate.
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph. The test set remains untouched (p.567).

questions.question: Why does get_best_epoch use patience=10 instead of the patience=5 used during the search?
questions.answer: The aggressive patience saved time during the search but may lead to underfitted models (stopping during a temporary plateau). A higher patience finds the true minimum of the validation loss more reliably.
questions.explanation: From the second paragraph and the 'Note the very high patience value' callout.

questions.question: history.history['val_loss'] = [0.40, 0.28, 0.21, 0.19, 0.20, 0.22]. What does get_best_epoch return, and how many epochs will get_best_trained_model train for?
questions.answer: best_epoch = 4 (min 0.19 at index 3, +1). Final training: int(4 × 1.2) = int(4.8) = 4 epochs.
questions.explanation: The index of the minimum is 3; adding 1 converts to an epoch count. p.569 multiplies by 1.2 and truncates with int().

questions.question: Where does the factor '20% more' come from?
questions.answer: The final training set has 60,000 samples versus 50,000 during the search and epoch selection: 60,000 / 50,000 = 1.2.
questions.explanation: The 10,000 validation samples are added back (p.567 split).

questions.question: Why can't EarlyStopping be used to decide the training length of the final full-data model?
options: EarlyStopping only works with KerasTuner
There is no held-out validation set left to monitor
The final model has no loss function
EarlyStopping is incompatible with batch_size=128
questions.answer: There is no held-out validation set left to monitor
questions.explanation: All 60k training samples are used for training. Monitoring the test set would leak it. The other options are false.

questions.question: Can you explain why the epoch count is decided before merging the validation data into training, and what would go wrong if you skipped this step?
questions.answer: Without validation data during the final run, you need the epoch count fixed in advance. Skipping it means guessing (risking under- or overfitting) or peeking at the test set (leaking it).
questions.explanation: The book's recipe uses the validation set one last time to settle this last parameter.

questions.question: Why might models from tuner.get_best_models(top_n) slightly underperform compared with the retrained ones?
options: They use a different architecture
They were trained during the search on less data and with aggressive early stopping
Their weights are randomly re-initialized
They are evaluated on the validation set instead of the test set
questions.answer: They were trained during the search on less data and with aggressive early stopping
questions.explanation: They were trained on the 50k split with patience=5 (p.567–568), while retraining uses 60k samples and a carefully chosen epoch count. Architecture is identical, weights are the saved ones (not re-initialized), and where you evaluate does not change model quality.

questions.question: Explain in your own words why automated hyperparameter optimization 'quickly overfits' the validation data.
questions.answer: Each trial's selection uses validation scores, so hyperparameters are effectively trained on the validation set. With many trials, configurations that happen to do well on that particular sample by chance get selected, so validation performance overstates generalization.
questions.explanation: This is the NOTE on the page, building on the information-leak discussion of p.173.

questions.question: A search space has 6 hyperparameters with 4, 3, 5, 2, 2 and 10 options. How many configurations does it contain? What fraction does a 50-trial budget cover?
questions.answer: 4·3·5·2·2·10 = 2,400 configurations; 50 trials cover about 2.1%.
questions.explanation: Search-space size is the product of option counts, which illustrates the combinatorial growth mentioned in the book.

questions.question: In the retraining loop, where is the test set used, and why only there?
questions.answer: Only in model.evaluate(x_test, y_test) after each model is fully trained. Using it earlier for any decision would leak it and bias the reported test metrics.
questions.explanation: See p.567's warning and the NOTE on validation overfitting.

questions.question: What does the book mean by 'Hyperparameter tuning is automation, not magic'?
options: Tuners only work on MNIST
Tuning automates experiments you'd otherwise run by hand, but you must still choose a sensible search space
Tuning should be avoided in favor of manual search
Tuners can design entirely new architectures without any input
questions.answer: Tuning automates experiments you'd otherwise run by hand, but you must still choose a sensible search space
questions.explanation: The book says you still need to handpick configurations with potential. It does not limit tuners to MNIST, argues for tuning rather than against it, and denies the 'magic' of option 4.

questions.question: What analogy do the authors use to argue that architectures should be optimized rather than hand-crafted?
questions.answer: The shift from hand-crafted features in shallow ML to features learned from a feedback signal in deep learning. Architectures should likewise be optimized in a principled way rather than hand-tuned.
questions.explanation: From the first paragraph of 'The art of crafting the right search space'.

questions.question: Give one micro-decision and one higher-level architecture decision you might put in a search space for an image classifier.
questions.answer: Micro: number of filters in the third conv layer. Higher-level: whether to use residual connections throughout, or whether to use batch normalization.
questions.explanation: The book's examples are 'what number of units' vs 'should I use residual connections throughout this model'.

questions.question: Why does KerasTuner provide premade search spaces such as HyperResNet?
options: Because micro-decisions transfer perfectly between datasets
Because higher-level architecture decisions generalize across tasks, so one template serves a broad problem category
Because ResNet cannot be built manually in Keras
Because premade spaces avoid validation-set overfitting
questions.answer: Because higher-level architecture decisions generalize across tasks, so one template serves a broad problem category
questions.explanation: The page says higher-level decisions generalize better and image classification problems share a search-space template. Micro-decisions are task-specific, ResNet can be built manually, and validation overfitting still applies.

questions.question: Define model ensembling in one sentence.
questions.answer: Pooling together the predictions of a set of different models to produce better predictions.
questions.explanation: The book's definition in section 18.1.2.

questions.question: What assumption does ensembling rely on, and how does the blind-men parable illustrate it?
questions.answer: Different well-performing models trained independently are good for different reasons, each capturing part of the truth. Each blind man touches a different part of the elephant; none is fully right, but together their descriptions are accurate.
questions.explanation: The parable maps men to models, and their touch points to the assumptions from architecture and initialization.

questions.question: Three classifiers output (0.6, 0.4), (0.3, 0.7) and (0.9, 0.1) for a binary problem. What is the equal-weight ensemble prediction and the chosen class?
questions.explanation: Average each class probability across models, then take the argmax.

questions.question: According to the book, what gives each 'blind man' (model) its unique perspective?
options: Being trained on a different test set
Its unique architecture and unique random weight initialization
Using a different loss for each class
Seeing the data in a different file format
questions.answer: Its unique architecture and unique random weight initialization
questions.explanation: Stated explicitly in the parable paragraph. Test sets are never used for training, and the other options are not mentioned.

questions.question: Can you predict when averaging four models would not improve over the best one? (Check p.571.)
questions.answer: When one model is much worse than the others, or when the models are nearly identical (low diversity) so their errors don't cancel.
questions.explanation: p.571 covers both the unequal-quality caveat and the diversity requirement.

questions.question: When can a simple equal-weight average fail to beat the best individual classifier?
options: When the classifiers are all equally good
When one classifier is significantly worse than the others
When there are more than two classes
When predictions are computed on validation data
questions.answer: When one classifier is significantly worse than the others
questions.explanation: The book states that averaging works only if classifiers are more or less equally good. Equal quality is the favourable case, and the number of classes and data split are irrelevant.

questions.question: On what data are ensemble weights learned, and with which methods does the book suggest searching for them?
questions.answer: On the validation data, using random search or a simple optimizer such as Nelder-Mead.
questions.explanation: Stated in the second paragraph; the callout says the weights in the code are assumed to be learned empirically.

questions.question: Using the book's weights (0.5, 0.25, 0.1, 0.15), compute the class-1 probability when models a–d predict class 1 with probabilities 0.2, 0.6, 0.9, 0.7.
questions.explanation: A weighted sum with weights adding to 1. The equal-weight average would be 0.6, which shows how the weighting favours model a.

questions.question: Why does ensembling the same architecture trained from different random initializations give only a tiny improvement?
questions.answer: The models are low in diversity: they learn very similar functions and make highly correlated errors (shared biases), so averaging cancels little.
questions.explanation: The book says if the only differences are initialization and data order, the ensemble is low in diversity.

questions.question: In the Higgs Boson challenge anecdote, why did the regularized greedy forest improve the ensemble by a large factor despite its worse score?
options: It was given the largest weight
It was so different from the other models that it provided information they lacked
It was trained on the test set
It was a deeper neural network than the others
questions.answer: It was so different from the other models that it provided information they lacked
questions.explanation: It got a small weight but added diversity (the explanation completes on p.572). It was a tree method, not a neural network, and nothing suggests test-set training.

questions.question: Explain 'if your models are biased in different ways, the biases will cancel each other out' using the blind-men parable.
questions.answer: If each man touches a different part, the trunk-touchers' 'snake' and the leg-touchers' 'pillar' errors offset each other in the combined description. If all touch the trunk, everyone says 'snake' and the shared error remains.
questions.explanation: This is the book's own use of the parable in the diversity paragraph.

questions.question: For a tabular prediction problem, which members would you choose for a diverse ensemble, following the book's advice?
questions.answer: For example, a gradient-boosted tree model, a random forest and a deep neural network, each tuned to be as good as possible, combined with weights learned on validation data.
questions.explanation: The author reports tree-based methods plus deep nets working well, while noting it does not generalize to every domain.

questions.question: According to the book, when is model parallelism used in practice?
options: Whenever you have more than one GPU
Only when the model is too large to fit on any single device
Only during inference
Whenever the batch size exceeds 128
questions.answer: Only when the model is too large to fit on any single device
questions.explanation: The page says model parallelism is used only for models too large for one device, as a way to train larger models. Having several GPUs alone calls for data parallelism. Inference and batch size are not the criteria.

questions.question: In data parallelism, what is replicated and what is split?
questions.answer: The model is replicated on every device. The data (each batch) is split so that each replica processes different samples.
questions.explanation: This is the definition in e10, expanded on p.573.

questions.question: Why does the book argue that faster training directly improves the quality of deep learning solutions?
questions.answer: Model quality comes from many refinement cycles of the loop of progress. Once writing experiments is fast, training time limits how many cycles you can do, so shorter runs (10-15 minutes) allow dozens of iterations a day and more refinement.
questions.explanation: This follows the e05/e07 reasoning around figure 18.1.

questions.question: Which tool does figure 18.1 attach to the 'Results -> Idea' arrow?
options: Keras
GPUs, TPUs
TensorBoard
KerasTuner
questions.answer: TensorBoard
questions.explanation: Figure 18.1 labels Idea->Experiment with Keras, Experiment->Results with GPUs/TPUs, and Results->Idea with the visualization framework TensorBoard. KerasTuner is not in the figure.

questions.question: Which kind of architecture does the book say suits model parallelism best, and why?
questions.answer: Models with a naturally parallel architecture, such as multi-branch models, because separate branches can run on separate devices at the same time with little dependence on each other.
questions.explanation: Stated in e10. The 'why' is the natural reading: independent branches need little communication between devices.

questions.question: If a model is split across 4 devices and that split model is replicated twice, how many devices are used, and which form of parallelism does each factor correspond to?
questions.answer: 8 devices. The factor 4 is model parallelism (split within a replica) and the factor 2 is data parallelism (number of replicas).
questions.explanation: Last sentence of the page, completed on p.573 (2 * 4 = 8).

questions.question: Think of your last project: which arrow of the loop of progress was your real bottleneck? Would multiple GPUs have helped?
questions.answer: Open answer. If runs took hours, multi-GPU data parallelism would help. If analysis or setup was slow, better tooling (Keras, TensorBoard) matters more.
questions.explanation: The book's point is to find and attack the slowest stage of the loop.

questions.question: With 4 GPUs and a global batch of 256 under data parallelism, what does each replica process per step?
options: The full batch of 256
A sub-batch of 64
A quarter of the model's layers
A sub-batch of 1024
questions.answer: A sub-batch of 64
questions.explanation: The batch is split into N = 4 sub-batches of 256 / 4 = 64. Processing the full batch would duplicate work. Splitting layers is model parallelism. 1024 confuses splitting with multiplying.

questions.question: How are results merged in data-parallel inference versus training?
questions.answer: Inference: concatenate the per-sub-batch predictions. Training: average the per-sub-batch gradients and apply that average to every replica.
questions.explanation: These are the two bullets on the page.

questions.question: Compute the number of parameters in the second Dense layer of Listing 18.4.
questions.explanation: Kernel (64000, 8000) plus bias (8000,), consistent with the 'about 512 million' on p.574.

questions.question: Why is synchronous data-parallel training equivalent to training on the full batch?
questions.answer: The loss is a mean over samples and gradients are linear, so averaging the gradients of equal-size sub-batch mean losses gives exactly the gradient of the full-batch mean loss. All replicas apply this same update to the same weights, so they stay identical.
questions.explanation: See math m1. The book states the equivalence; the derivation is added here.

questions.question: What is the stated limitation of data parallelism?
options: It cannot be used for inference
It requires the model to fit on a single device
It only works with two GPUs
Replicas drift apart over time
questions.answer: It requires the model to fit on a single device
questions.explanation: The book names exactly this. Inference works by concatenation, it scales beyond two GPUs, and synchronous training keeps replicas in sync.

questions.question: Why does Listing 18.4 use a sigmoid output instead of softmax?
questions.answer: The 8,000 categories are 'potentially overlapping' (multi-label), so each needs an independent probability. Softmax would force the outputs to compete and sum to 1.
questions.explanation: Follows from the text in e14 and the activation in the listing.

questions.question: Can you explain to a colleague, without notes, the difference between a replica, a sub-batch, and the global batch?
questions.answer: Replica = full model copy on one device; sub-batch = slice of data one replica processes; global batch = all sub-batches together, i.e., what one optimizer step sees.
questions.explanation: If any of these was unclear, reread the first paragraph of the data parallelism subsection.

questions.question: Splitting Dense(64000) with a (16000, 64000) kernel across four devices along the last axis gives per-device kernels of shape:
questions.explanation: The last axis is divided by 4: 64000 / 4 = 16000, and the input axis stays 16000. (16000, 32000) is the two-device case from the page. The other options split the wrong axis.

questions.question: What is the main drawback of horizontal partitioning according to the book?
questions.answer: Communication overhead: one layer's output must be copied to the next device before the next layer can run, which can become a bottleneck and leave GPUs idle.
questions.explanation: Stated in the horizontal partitioning paragraph.

questions.question: Show that concatenating x W_0 + b_0 and x W_1 + b_1 equals x W + b when W = [W_0 | W_1] and b = [b_0 | b_1].
questions.answer: Column j of xW is x times column j of W. The columns of W_0 are the first 32,000 columns of W, so x W_0 gives the first 32,000 columns of xW, and likewise for W_1. Adding the matching bias slices and placing the blocks side by side gives xW + b.
questions.explanation: See math m1, with a numerical check.

questions.question: Why is vertical partitioning easy to implement for typical layers?
questions.answer: Layers are mostly matmul or convolution operations, which are highly parallelizable: different output units or channels can be computed independently on different devices.
questions.explanation: This is the book's stated reason.

questions.question: In the mixed setup described on the page, how many devices does each model replica use, and how many replicas are there?
options: 2 devices, 4 replicas
4 devices, 2 replicas
8 devices, 1 replica
1 device, 8 replicas
questions.answer: 4 devices, 2 replicas
questions.explanation: Two replicas, each running on four devices, for a total of eight (figure 18.2). The other options either swap the roles or remove one form of parallelism.

questions.question: What line of code is missing from the printed snippet to finish the layer computation?
questions.answer: A concatenation, e.g. output = keras.ops.concatenate([half_output_0, half_output_1], axis=-1) (followed by the ReLU activation for this layer).
questions.explanation: The text announces concatenation but the snippet stops after computing the halves.

questions.question: Why does the book choose the JAX backend for distributed training?
questions.answer: The authors consider it by far the most performant and scalable Keras backend for large-scale distributed training; not using it wastes compute and money (p.575).
questions.explanation: From e08 and its continuation.

questions.question: Could you sketch on paper which device holds which slice of W1 and W2 when vertically partitioning both Dense layers of Listing 18.4 over two GPUs?
questions.answer: Self-check: W1 split by columns (16000 x 32000 each); W2 split by rows (32000 x 8000 each) matching each GPU's hidden units, with partial outputs summed, or by columns with the hidden activations gathered first.
questions.explanation: The second layer's split is beyond the page; see the 'Horizontal vs vertical' deeper note.

questions.question: Where must keras.distribution.set_distribution(...) be called?
options: After model.fit()
Before building the model
Inside the model's call() method
After model.compile() but before fit()
questions.answer: Before building the model
questions.explanation: The book says 'before building your model', because variables must be created with the distribution's layout. Calling it later would leave existing variables on a single device.

questions.question: What does keras.distribution.list_devices() return?
questions.answer: A list of device-name strings such as "gpu:0", "gpu:1".
questions.explanation: As stated on the page.

questions.question: In figure 18.2, what is a 'local batch' and how does it relate to the global batch?
questions.answer: Each local batch is the part of the global batch sent to one model replica. With two replicas, the global batch is split in two, and each half is processed by a group of four GPUs.
questions.explanation: The figure shows two 'Local batch' arrows coming out of the 'Global batch'.

questions.question: Which hardware option does the book recommend for most people?
options: Build a workstation with eight GPUs
Use the free Colab GPU
Rent a multi-GPU VM on a cloud provider
Use the CPU with more threads
questions.answer: Rent a multi-GPU VM on a cloud provider
questions.explanation: The book calls renting likely the best option unless you train 24/7. Building is not the best option for most people, and Colab has a single GPU. CPUs are not discussed.

questions.question: Why can a single line of configuration give multi-GPU training without changing the model or fit() code?
questions.answer: The distribution decides how variables are placed (replicated) and how input batches are split, and the JAX/XLA compiler inserts the required communication (gradient averaging). The model logic itself is unchanged.
questions.explanation: Combines the book's one-line claim with the mechanism described on p.573 and p.577.

questions.question: How many model replicas does figure 18.2 show, and which GPUs belong to each?
questions.answer: Two replicas: GPU:0-GPU:3 and GPU:4-GPU:7 (both are printed as 'Model replica 0', but the second is replica 1).
questions.explanation: Read from the figure.

questions.question: Do you know how you would run this on a cloud VM: which backend environment variable to set and which line to add?
questions.answer: Set KERAS_BACKEND=jax before importing Keras, then call keras.distribution.set_distribution(keras.distribution.DataParallel()) before building the model.
questions.explanation: If unsure, revisit the 'Using data parallelism with JAX' subsection.

questions.question: Using the book's numbers, what is the scaling efficiency on 4 and on 8 GPUs?
questions.explanation: Efficiency = speedup / N (math m1).

questions.question: What does the book identify as the main source of distribution overhead?
options: Loading data from disk
Merging the weight deltas from different devices
Compiling the model
Python interpreter overhead
questions.answer: Merging the weight deltas from different devices
questions.explanation: Stated directly. The other options are real overheads in general but not the one the book names.

questions.question: Why can multi-GPU training disappoint with a small batch size?
questions.answer: The global batch is split across GPUs. If it is small, each local batch is too small to saturate a GPU, so devices are under-used and fixed overheads dominate.
questions.explanation: From e07.

questions.question: In DeviceMesh(shape=(2, 4), axis_names=["data", "model"]), how many model replicas are there?
questions.explanation: The data axis has size 2, so there are two replicas, each sharded over the 4 devices of the model axis (p.577). 4 is the model-sharding degree and 8 is the total device count.

questions.question: In figure 18.2's grid, which axis handles data parallelism and which handles model parallelism?
questions.answer: Horizontal axis (across the two replica groups) = data parallelism; vertical axis (within a group) = model parallelism.
questions.explanation: As stated in e13.

questions.question: Why is it useful to give mesh axes names like "data" and "model"?
questions.answer: Layouts can then refer to axes by meaning (e.g., shard a variable dimension along "model") rather than by position or device count, which keeps sharding specifications readable and portable.
questions.explanation: The callout says naming is convenient; the LayoutMap on p.577 uses the name "model".

questions.question: Could you choose a mesh shape for 16 GPUs where each replica needs 4 GPUs to fit the model?
questions.answer: shape=(4, 4) with axis_names=["data", "model"]: 4 replicas, each sharded 4 ways.
questions.explanation: Product must be 16; the model axis is set by memory needs and the data axis gets the rest.

questions.question: A variable of shape (32, 64) with layout (None, "model") on a mesh whose model axis has 4 devices: what shape does each device on that axis hold?
questions.explanation: None keeps dimension 0 (32) whole; "model" splits dimension 1 by 4 (64/4 = 16). (8, 64) would be ("model", None), (32, 64) fully replicated, and (8, 16) would split both dimensions over the same 4 devices, which is not a valid single-axis layout.

questions.question: What does None mean in a LayoutMap tuple?
questions.answer: Replicate the variable along this dimension (the full dimension is present on every device).
questions.explanation: Printed callout.

questions.question: Why does the bias layout ("model",) match the kernel layout (None, "model")?
questions.answer: The kernel is split along its output-units dimension, so each device computes a slice of the output units. The bias has one entry per output unit, so it must be split the same way for each device to add the right bias slice to its output slice.
questions.explanation: Same reasoning as the half-kernel/half-bias pairing on p.574.

questions.question: In DeviceMesh(shape=(2, 4), axis_names=["data", "model"], devices=[gpu:0..gpu:7]), which GPUs form model replica 0 (assuming row-major ordering)?
options: gpu:0, gpu:2, gpu:4, gpu:6
gpu:0-gpu:3
gpu:0 and gpu:4
gpu:4-gpu:7
questions.answer: gpu:0-gpu:3
questions.explanation: The first 4 devices fill data index 0 across the 4 model positions, matching figure 18.2. gpu:0 and gpu:4 are the same shard in two different replicas. gpu:4-7 is replica 1.

questions.question: Why does Keras use variables as the frame of reference for distribution?
questions.answer: Once variables are split or replicated across devices, the compiler can move the computation associated with each part of a variable to the device that holds it. You only annotate weights, and model and training code stay unchanged.
questions.explanation: From e07 and p.578.

questions.question: On the 2 x 4 mesh, how many parameters of Listing 18.4's first kernel does each GPU hold with layout (None, "model")?
questions.answer: 16000 x (64000 / 4) = 256,000,000 parameters (about 1.02 GB in float32).
questions.explanation: Shard the last dimension by the model-axis size 4; the data axis replicates.

questions.question: Can you write the LayoutMap entries for a Dense layer whose variable path prefix is "sequential/dense", sharding its output units along "model"?
questions.answer: "sequential/dense/kernel": (None, "model") and "sequential/dense/bias": ("model",).
questions.explanation: Same pattern as the printed example.

questions.question: What layout does the book assign to `sequential/dense/bias`?
options: (None,)
("model",)
(None, "model")
("data",)
questions.answer: ("model",)
questions.explanation: Biases have one dimension, which is also their last, so by the rule of thumb it is sharded on the model axis. (None,) would replicate it; (None, "model") has the wrong rank; "data" is the batch axis, not used for weights.

questions.question: On the 2 x 4 mesh, what shape does each device hold for `sequential/dense_1/kernel` (full shape (64000, 8000)) under the layout (None, "model")?
questions.explanation: The first dimension is replicated (None), and the last is split across the 4 devices of the model axis: 8000 / 4 = 2000.

questions.question: Why does the LayoutMap use string variable paths rather than references to the variable objects?
questions.answer: Because the layout must be known before the variables are created: set_distribution is called before building the model so variables are instantiated already sharded. A path can be written before the object exists.
questions.explanation: The page says the path is a way to refer to a variable without keeping a handle on the instance, and the distribution is used 'when instantiating the variables'.

questions.question: What does `batch_dim_name="data"` do in `ModelParallel`?
options: Names the dataset to load
Tells Keras to split the batch dimension along the mesh axis named "data" (data parallelism)
Shards weights along the data axis
Sets the batch size
questions.answer: Tells Keras to split the batch dimension along the mesh axis named "data" (data parallelism)
questions.explanation: The margin callout says the argument tells Keras to use the mesh axis named "data" for data parallelism. It names a mesh axis, not a dataset or a batch size, and weights are sharded along "model".

questions.question: What must change in your model-building and `fit()` code once a ModelParallel distribution is set?
questions.answer: Nothing. Model definition and training code (fit/evaluate or a custom loop) stay the same.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph states this explicitly; distribution is purely configuration.

questions.question: Roughly how many parameters of `sequential/dense/kernel` does each device store on the 2 x 4 mesh?
questions.explanation: Full kernel 16000 x 64000 = 1.024 B; split four ways along the last axis gives 256 M. Devices in the other data row hold duplicates.

questions.question: Can you write, from memory, the four lines that build the LayoutMap for listing 18.4 and the two calls that activate it?
questions.answer: LayoutMap(device_mesh); kernels -> (None, "model"); biases -> ("model",); ModelParallel(layout_map=layout_map, batch_dim_name="data"); keras.distribution.set_distribution(model_parallel).
questions.explanation: If you can reproduce this, you have the full recipe from this page.

questions.question: What does `PartitionSpec(None, "model")` mean for the (16000, 64000) kernel?
options: Both dimensions are sharded
Rows are replicated; columns are split across the model axis
Rows are split across the model axis; columns replicated
The kernel is only stored on the model devices of the first data row
questions.answer: Rows are replicated; columns are split across the model axis
questions.explanation: Each spec entry refers to one dimension: None means replicated and "model" means sharded over the model axis. The data axis is unmentioned, so the kernel is replicated across both data rows, which rules out the last option.

questions.question: Which attribute chain does the book use to inspect the sharding of the first layer's kernel?
questions.answer: model.layers[0].kernel.value.sharding
questions.explanation: `.value` exposes the backend jax.Array, which carries `.sharding`.

questions.question: Why does prefetching help especially in distributed training?
questions.answer: More devices consume batches faster, so the host input pipeline easily becomes the bottleneck. Prefetching overlaps preparing the next batches with the current computation, so devices don't sit idle.
questions.explanation: The sidebar recommends tf.data plus prefetch for best performance in distributed training.

questions.question: What is an ASIC?
options: A general-purpose graphics processor
An application-specific integrated circuit designed for one kind of workload
A software library for distributed training
A Keras distribution strategy
questions.answer: An application-specific integrated circuit designed for one kind of workload
questions.explanation: The page defines single-purpose deep-learning chips as ASICs (application-specific integrated circuits), with the TPU as the main example. GPUs are general purpose, and the other two options are software.

questions.question: According to the book, how does TPU v2 compare to an NVIDIA P100 in speed and cost-effectiveness?
questions.answer: Typically 15x faster, and about 3x more cost-effective on average for most models.
questions.explanation: Both figures are stated in the TPU training paragraph.

questions.question: If one of your LayoutMap paths had a typo, how would you notice it using the tools on this page?
questions.answer: Inspect `.value.sharding` (or visualize_sharding) for each variable. The misnamed variable would not show the intended PartitionSpec and would appear unsharded/replicated.
questions.explanation: Inspecting shardings is the debugging tool introduced on this page.

questions.question: What does `steps_per_execution=8` in `compile()` do?
options: Multiplies the batch size by 8
Runs eight training steps per TPU execution, reducing host-device round trips
Trains for 8 epochs
Uses 8 TPU cores
questions.answer: Runs eight training steps per TPU execution, reducing host-device round trips
questions.explanation: That is step fusing as described on the page. The batch size is unchanged, epochs are set in fit(), and core usage depends on the distribution.

questions.question: Why should you raise the learning rate when training with enormous batches?
questions.answer: You make fewer updates per epoch, but each gradient is more accurate (averaged over more samples), so each update can and should move the weights by a larger amount.
questions.explanation: This is the authors' reasoning in the step-fusing subsection.

questions.question: What does the NOTE recommend if reading data from Google Cloud Storage is slowing down TPU training and the dataset is small?
questions.answer: Keep it in VM memory by calling dataset.cache() on the tf.data.Dataset, so it is read from GCS only once.
questions.explanation: TPUs consume batches very quickly, so I/O becomes the bottleneck.

questions.question: When must keras.distribution.set_distribution be called on a TPU notebook?
options: After model.fit()
Before creating the model
After compile() but before fit()
Any time; it is retroactive
questions.answer: Before creating the model
questions.explanation: The page says 'Make sure to call it before creating your model!' because variables are placed when they are created. The other options all come after the variables already exist.

questions.question: What analogy does the book use for numerical precision, and what does it imply?
questions.answer: Precision is to numbers what resolution is to images: more bits let you distinguish values that are closer together, just as more pixels show finer detail.
questions.explanation: Stated at the start of 18.3.1.

questions.question: What speedup does the book promise from the lower-precision technique introduced in 18.3?
questions.answer: Up to 2x for training and inference of almost any model, basically for free.
questions.explanation: Stated in the section introduction.

questions.question: Can you explain to a colleague the difference between using a bigger batch and using step fusing to improve TPU utilization?
questions.answer: A bigger batch changes the optimization (fewer, more accurate updates; needs a higher LR). Step fusing keeps batch size and update count the same but runs several steps per device call to avoid round-trip overhead.
questions.explanation: Both are presented on this page as ways to keep the TPU busy.

questions.question: In float32, what is the actual (unbiased) exponent when the stored exponent bits are 10000000?
questions.explanation: 10000000₂ = 128, and the bias is 127, so 128 − 127 = 1. 128 is the stored value before removing the bias; 0 would need stored bits 01111111; −127 is the bias itself.

questions.question: Using the book's template, compute the value of a float32 with sign bit 1, stored exponent 129 and significand 1.25.
Why does a float format have the same number of representable values between 1024 and 2048 as between 1 and 2?
questions.answer: Each interval corresponds to one exponent value, and for a fixed exponent the mantissa provides the same fixed number of evenly spaced points (2^23 in float32), whatever the width of the interval.
questions.explanation: This follows from the sign/exponent/mantissa encoding in the sidebar.

questions.question: What is the range of signed 32-bit integers stated in the book?
questions.explanation: That is −2^31 to 2^31 − 1.

questions.question: How many bits are allocated to the sign, exponent and mantissa in float32 (figure 18.3)?
questions.explanation: Figure 18.3 shows 1 + 8 + 23 = 32 bits. 1/5/10 is float16, 1/8/7 is bfloat16 (table 18.1, p.583), and 1/11/52 is float64.

questions.question: The mantissa bits of float32(π) read as an integer equal 4,788,187. Verify that the significand is about 1.5708.
questions.explanation: The significand is 1 plus the mantissa integer divided by 2^23; times 2^1 gives ≈ 3.14159274.

questions.question: Could you explain to someone why rounding errors get larger for bigger numbers in floating point?
questions.answer: Because spacing between representable values doubles with each power of two (same count per binade), the maximum rounding error, half the spacing, grows proportionally with magnitude.
questions.explanation: This is the sidebar's main point, continued on p.582.

questions.question: Compared with float16, bfloat16 has...
options: more mantissa bits and fewer exponent bits
more exponent bits and fewer mantissa bits
the same bits but a different bias
32 bits in total
questions.answer: more exponent bits and fewer mantissa bits
questions.explanation: 8 exponent vs 5 and 7 mantissa vs 10, giving wider range and lower resolution. The first option describes the reverse; the third is wrong because the field widths differ; both formats are 16 bits.

questions.question: What approximate resolution does the book give for half, single and double precision?
questions.answer: Half: 1e-3; single: 1e-7; double: 1e-16.
questions.explanation: Stated right after the sidebar; these match the machine epsilons 2^-10, 2^-23, 2^-52.

questions.question: A float16 weight equals 1.0 and the optimizer computes an update of +2e-4. What does the weight become in float16, and why?
questions.answer: It stays 1.0, because the float16 spacing near 1 is 2^-10 ≈ 9.8e-4 and 2e-4 is less than half of it, so 1.0002 rounds back to 1.0.
questions.explanation: This is the reason float16 cannot hold weights during training.

questions.question: Why must `set_dtype_policy` be called before defining the model?
questions.answer: Layers read the global policy when they are constructed (creating their variables and choosing compute dtype). Layers built earlier keep their old dtype.
questions.explanation: The page says 'this should be done before you define your model'.

questions.question: What speedup does the book say to expect from float16 inference on GPU and TPU?
options: About 10%
Nearly 2x
About 4x
None; it only saves memory
questions.answer: Nearly 2x
questions.explanation: The page says you should expect 'a nearly 2× speed boost on GPU and TPU'. 10% understates it, 4x overstates it, and the speed gain, not just memory saving, is the point.

questions.question: Why might bfloat16 be preferred on TPUs or for large models, despite its lower resolution?
questions.answer: Some hardware (notably TPUs) is better optimized for it, and its 8-bit exponent gives float32-like range, so values rarely overflow or underflow.
questions.explanation: The page notes wider range and device optimization, and advises trying both.

questions.question: Can you explain why float16 is fine for inference but not for storing weights during training?
questions.answer: Inference needs no tiny updates, and 3 significant digits are enough for activations. Training applies updates of ~1e-6, far below float16's ~1e-3 relative resolution, so they would be rounded away.
questions.explanation: Combines the resolution paragraph with the float16 inference paragraph.

questions.question: Under the "mixed_float16" policy, what are a typical layer's variable_dtype and compute_dtype?
options: float16 and float16
float32 and float16
float16 and float32
float32 and float32
questions.answer: float32 and float16
questions.explanation: Variables stay float32 for accurate updates, and computation switches to float16 for speed. Pure float16 is the inference policy; float32/float32 is the default; the reversed pair makes no sense for speed.

questions.question: How do you keep a specific layer (e.g. the softmax output) in full precision under mixed precision?
questions.answer: Pass dtype="float32" to the layer's constructor.
questions.explanation: Stated at the end of 18.3.3.

questions.question: Why are float16 gradients cast to float32 before the optimizer update?
questions.answer: So the update is applied to float32 variables with float32 resolution, where small steps (~1e-6) aren't rounded away as they would be at float16's ~1e-3 resolution.
questions.explanation: This is the core idea of mixed precision on this page.

questions.question: According to table 18.1, how many mantissa bits does bfloat16 have?
questions.explanation: bfloat16 has 8 exponent and 7 mantissa bits. 5 and 10 are float16's exponent and mantissa counts; 8 is bfloat16's exponent count.

questions.question: In float16 the spacing between numbers near 1 is about 9.8e-4. With a weight of 1.0 and an update of 1e-5, what is the result if the update is applied in float16 versus in float32?
questions.answer: float16: 1.0 (unchanged, since 1e-5 < half the spacing); float32: 0.99999 (the spacing near 1 is ~1.2e-7, so the update is kept).
questions.explanation: This shows why mixed precision keeps variables in float32.

questions.question: What new problem does section 18.3.4 point out, even with float32 variables?
questions.answer: Gradients themselves are still float16, so very small gradients can fall outside float16's representable range and be rounded to zero, preventing learning. Loss scaling addresses this.
questions.explanation: The page ends by stating the gradients remain in float16 and the limited range can round them to zero (continued on p.584).

questions.question: Can you draw the flow of dtypes through one mixed-precision training step, from stored weight to updated weight?
questions.answer: float32 weight → float16 copy → float16 forward (softmax in float32) → float16 gradient → cast to float32 → float32 update of the float32 weight.
questions.explanation: Compare your sketch with the mermaid diagram on this page.

questions.question: Why does multiplying the loss by a constant help float16 training?
options: It increases the effective learning rate
Gradients scale by the same constant, so small ones no longer underflow to zero
It reduces the number of mantissa bits needed
It makes the loss converge to a lower value
questions.answer: Gradients scale by the same constant, so small ones no longer underflow to zero
questions.explanation: Gradients are proportional to the loss (linearity of differentiation). The learning rate is unaffected because gradients are unscaled before the update; mantissa bits are fixed by the format; the optimum is unchanged.

questions.question: Why does the book recommend `LossScaleOptimizer` over a fixed `loss_scale_factor`?
questions.answer: Because the right scaling value can change over the course of training, and the wrapper figures it out automatically.
questions.explanation: Stated directly on the page. Gradient magnitudes drift during training, so any fixed factor may become too small (underflow) or too large (overflow).

questions.question: float16's smallest positive subnormal is about 6e-8. A gradient entry is 1e-9. What is the smallest power-of-two loss scale that makes the scaled value at least 6e-8, and what value is passed to the update after unscaling?
questions.answer: s = 64 (2^6), giving 6.4e-8; after dividing by 64 in float32 the update uses about 1e-9.
questions.explanation: We need s >= 60; the smallest power of two is 64. In practice much larger scales (e.g. 2^15) are used to keep values in the normal range with full precision. The divide happens in float32, so 1e-9 is recovered.

questions.question: Which Keras layers does the built-in float8 training implementation cover?
options: All layers, via compute_dtype='float8'
Conv2D, Dense and LSTM
Dense, EinsumDense and Embedding
Only MultiHeadAttention
questions.answer: Dense, EinsumDense and Embedding
questions.explanation: The page lists exactly these three, targeting Transformers. compute_dtype='float8' is explicitly said not to work; Conv2D/LSTM are not mentioned; MultiHeadAttention is covered indirectly through EinsumDense.

questions.question: Why can float8 training make a model train slower than float16 mixed precision?
questions.answer: Float8 needs extra work (tracking past activation values, rescaling activations and gradients, overriding part of the backward pass). On small models or weaker GPUs that overhead costs more than the faster float8 matmuls save.
questions.explanation: The page says the added overhead has a computational cost that can exceed the benefits; p.585 adds that it is viable only for very large models on recent GPUs.

questions.question: Why is float16 described as the last precision level that 'just works'?
questions.answer: It has enough bits to represent all intermediate tensors of the forward pass by simple casting (with float32 only for gradient updates); float8 loses too much information for plain casting.
questions.explanation: Direct paraphrase of the page. The contrast is that float8 requires modifying the computation with scale factors, not just changing dtypes.

questions.question: Could you explain to a colleague, without notes, how a single training step with dynamic loss scaling proceeds, including what happens when a gradient overflows?
questions.answer: Scale loss, backprop, unscale in float32, check finiteness, apply or skip, adjust the scale.
questions.explanation: Compare your explanation with diagram v1. The overflow handling is beyond the book's text but is what LossScaleOptimizer does.

questions.question: Why can the output of an int8 matmul be converted back to the correct float result?
options: Because int8 has the same range as float32
Because matmul is linear, so dividing by the product of the input scales cancels the scaling
Because the rounding errors cancel out on average
Because the kernel is stored in float32
questions.answer: Because matmul is linear, so dividing by the product of the input scales cancels the scaling
questions.explanation: This is the book's argument. int8's range is tiny; rounding errors do not cancel exactly (they are the residual error); the kernel is quantized to int8 too.

questions.question: Using abs-max scaling, compute the scale for kernel = [[-0.1, -2.2], [1.1, 0.7]] and its quantized values.
What does x become if cast directly to int8 without scaling, and why?
questions.answer: [[0, 0], [1, 0]], because casting truncates toward zero and most entries have magnitude below 1.
questions.explanation: Given on the page; truncation maps 0.1, 0.9 and -0.8 to 0 and 1.2 to 1.

questions.question: Why does abs_max_quantize round and clip before casting, instead of casting directly?
questions.answer: Casting truncates, introducing a bias toward zero and up to a full grid step of error; rounding gives at most half a step. Clipping guarantees values stay within [-127, 127].
questions.explanation: The callout says rounding and clipping first is more accurate than direct casting.

questions.question: According to the page, when is float8 training viable?
options: For any model on any modern GPU
For very large models (typically over 5B parameters) on recent GPUs such as the H100
Only for inference
For small models on CPUs
questions.answer: For very large models (typically over 5B parameters) on recent GPUs such as the H100
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph; the other options contradict the p.584 warning about overhead on small models and weaker hardware.

questions.question: The text says [-127, 127] is 'a total of 256 possible values'. Is that right?
questions.answer: No: [-127, 127] contains 255 integers. The int8 type has 256 values ([-128, 127]); the symmetric scheme leaves -128 unused.
questions.explanation: Count: 127 negatives + 0 + 127 positives = 255.

questions.question: Can you quantize x by hand with abs-max scaling and predict the integer tensor before reading p.586?
questions.explanation: Compare with the numerical example in math m1.

questions.question: Given int_x = [[11, 95], [127, -85]] and int_kernel = [[-6, -127], [64, 40]], compute int_y[1,1] and dequantize it with x_scale·kernel_scale ≈ 6109.4.
questions.explanation: Matches the printed -3.1965137 vs. exact -3.2.

questions.question: Which layers does Keras's built-in int8 quantization support, according to the page?
options: Conv2D, Dense, LSTM
Dense, EinsumDense, Embedding
All layers
Only Embedding
questions.answer: Dense, EinsumDense, Embedding
questions.explanation: The page lists these three, the same as for float8; that is why it says Transformer-based models are covered.

questions.question: Which elementwise ops does quantization add to the computation graph?
questions.answer: abs, max, clip, cast, divide, multiply.
questions.explanation: Listed on the page; they are cheap compared with the matmul.

questions.question: Why does the callout say predict() and call() run only 'partially' in int8 after model.quantize("int8")?
questions.answer: Only the quantizable layers (Dense, EinsumDense, Embedding) use int8; other operations such as normalization, activations and softmax still run in floating point, and inputs are dequantized after each int8 matmul.
questions.explanation: Follows from the restricted set of supported layers stated on the page.

questions.question: Why is quantization more worthwhile for a large matmul than for the 2x2 example?
questions.answer: The matmul cost grows as O(n^3) while the quantization overhead is elementwise, O(n^2); for large matrices the int8 speedup dominates.
questions.explanation: The page says that for a large matmul this saves a lot of compute, with only fast elementwise ops added.

questions.question: What would happen if you forgot to divide int_y by (x_scale * kernel_scale)?
options: Nothing; int_y already equals x @ kernel
The result would be about 6100 times too large
The result would be rounded to zero
The matmul would fail with a dtype error
questions.answer: The result would be about 6100 times too large
questions.explanation: int_y ≈ s_x s_W (x @ kernel) with s_x s_W ≈ 6109.4. No rounding to zero or dtype error is involved.

questions.question: Could you take a trained Keras Transformer, quantize it to int8, and design a check that its accuracy is still acceptable?
questions.answer: Call model.quantize("int8") and compare validation metrics (and outputs) with the float model.
questions.explanation: The page gives the API; validation is the practical safeguard implied by the y vs. exact comparison.

questions.question: When is model parallelism needed rather than data parallelism?
options: When the dataset is very large
When the model is too large to fit on a single device
When training on a CPU
When using mixed precision
questions.answer: When the model is too large to fit on a single device
questions.explanation: Data parallelism requires the model to fit on one device; dataset size is handled by data parallelism; CPU and mixed precision are unrelated.

questions.question: What is the risk the summary associates with hyperparameter tuning?
questions.answer: Validation-set overfitting.
questions.explanation: Repeatedly selecting configurations by their validation score makes the selection fit the validation set.

questions.question: Why does an ensemble need diverse models to help?
questions.answer: Averaging helps only if models make different errors that partially cancel; identical models make the same errors.
questions.explanation: The bullet specifies 'diverse models'; section 18.1.2 explains ensembling.

questions.question: Which two techniques does the summary name for speeding up inference?
options: Dropout and batch normalization
float16 precision and int8 quantization
Data parallelism and ensembling
float8 training and loss scaling
questions.answer: float16 precision and int8 quantization
questions.explanation: Last bullet. The others are regularization, training-scale, or training-precision techniques.

questions.question: Mixed precision is said to come 'at virtually no cost'. Which chapter mechanisms make that true?
questions.answer: Keeping weights and updates in float32, running numerically unstable ops like softmax in float32, and loss scaling for float16 gradients.
questions.explanation: Covered on pp.583-584.

questions.question: For a project of your own, which of the six techniques would you try first, and why?
questions.answer: Open-ended; e.g. mixed precision first because it is nearly free, then tuning.
questions.explanation: Use the decision guide in the deeper section.
